utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. A very good morning to everybody. Any obstacles to proceed immediately with the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if you can please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I only asked for obstacles before really starting because we should hear, no doubt, the case and the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, let's hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, may it please the Court, my name is Andrew Cayley, I appear on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor with my colleague Ann Sutherland and our case manager Miss Karper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. John Ostojic, along with Danilo Cirkovic on behalf of the accused Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. From this point of view, it gives a wrong impression, but just for the record, on the same line, so to speak, we have the same gentleman as yesterday. Could you please, for the record, give us the name again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HUDSON
utterances.text: Yes; Mr. John Hudson and Mr. Hedley Tomlyn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, as you know, time is short, and I would like to try and complete your examination-in-chief by the first break, if possible. So if you can keep answers fairly short, we don't have that many more documents to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could display the Omarska slide, and you could place on the ELMO the document that we were previously looking at. And you had read significant portions of this document. And for the interpreters, this document is ERN number 01108903, report by Prijedor Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are there any other parts of this particular report, Mr. Brown, to which you wish to draw the attention of the Judges? We were previously on page 3 of that document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would like just to draw your attention to the bottom paragraph and the part that I have highlighted here on page 3. This reads, in relation to Omarska camp: "For this reason, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor decided that all captives should be transferred from the Keraterm facility in Prijedor to the premises of the administration building and the workshop of the iron ore mine in Omarska where the mixed teams of operatives continued the processing they had started. For this reason, the facility got the working name of Omarska Prisoner of War Investigation Centre. By the same decision, the facility was placed under the control of the police and the army. The police were given the task of providing immediate physical security, and the army took over in-depth security in the form of two rings and the mining of prisoners' possible escape routes." On page 4 of document, I will not read it all out, however, the first section states: "In the same Crisis Staff decision, it was ordered that the Keraterm facility in Prijedor should be used only for transit purposes, and that only the first selection of persons brought in should be made there since for reasons of lack of space, this was not feasible in Prijedor SJB." And then it makes another reference to the decision of the 27th of May in relation to Omarska. It also indicates in the second paragraph the categorisation of prisoners, in essence, into those who had been personally responsible for the armed rebellion, those who had been suspected of organising, abetting, or financing the armed rebellion, and those who had no interest but had been captured because they were in the area of combat or in the area of fighting. The document also lists that from the 27th of May until the 16th of August, a total of 3.334 people had been brought to Omarska, and it makes some reference here to the breakdown. There is one or two other small sections on paragraph 6 -- sorry, page 6. This is in relation to a section on the activities of the police, and I just highlighted the fact showing the cooperation that existed between the police and the army. After the outbreak of the armed conflict, employees of the SJB, at the request of the army and as a result of the situation they found themselves in, took part in armed conflicts. And together with members of the military units, police employees have taken part in searches of the terrain and mopping up the remaining covert enemy groups and individuals. Those are some of the key issues in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go back to the slide, please, I think this slide essentially summarises the two previous documents we've referred to, the one we referred to today and yesterday, and the one before that. But if you could just go through that document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, through the slide?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Through the slide, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This just, I think, tries to encapsulate some of the documentation that we discussed yesterday: That prisoners were brought to Omarska as a result of the attacks and disarmament operations; that the camp was established by the Prijedor Crisis Staff in late May, 27th of May, as indicated in the police documents; that security coordinators, including military representation, Colonel Majstorovic, who was a security officer at Prijedor Garrison, were involved in the processing of prisoners; that the military provided external security to the camp; and that after interrogation or processing, there was a categorisation of prisoners. The prisoners themselves were eventually either sent to Trnopolje camp or sent on to Manjaca camp, which was a military detention facility in Banja Luka Municipality run by the 1st Krajina Corps. There's documentation, the police documentation that I've highlighted there, indicates that prisoners were transferred to Manjaca. It is also known from a military document in August, I believe August the 6th, that when they checked the prisoners in Manjaca, it was stated that a large number did not deserve to be treated as prisoners of war and did not deserve to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. President, I could apply for that document to be admitted into evidence, I think it would be 353. That's the report that we've just been referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Already been provisionally marked yesterday as 353. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted into evidence as 353.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next slide, Mr. Brown, Keraterm camp. And again, I think here you rely on a MUP report, and that if that could be placed on the ELMO and if you could highlight the relevant portions of that report. And this, for the benefit of the interpreters, is ERN 01108891.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, this is a document which states at the top: "Serbian Republic Ministry of the Interior Security Services Centre, Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the Banja Luka CSB's compilation of the reports that came from Prijedor Municipality, Sanski Most Municipality, and Bosanski Novi Municipality, in relation to the issues we discussed yesterday on detention camps and the role of the police and their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where did we get this document from?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was seized by the OTP in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you'd highlight the relevant portions for Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, the document is simply a summary, transferring on Prijedor Municipality's -- or the Prijedor SJB report, and it summarises very much the same material discussed in Drljaca's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's the previous document we have been referring to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you place a copy of this document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't read out the whole of the highlighted section, but you can see, for example, the part that relates to Trnopolje is very much the same as the section that related to -- that was lifted from the Prijedor report. I draw your attention to page 2 of the report in relation to Keraterm. Again, it highlights some details in relation to Keraterm and its makeup. It references, pursuant to the decision of the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff, the army brought prisoners of war to this facility. Highlights the roles of the SJB, indicates that both the CSB and Banja Luka Corps Command were informed about the capture of persons and were actively involved in the solution of the situation. References again mixed operational teams of public, military, and security service personnel. At the bottom of the document and on to the following page, page 3, again it references the 27th of May decision in relation to Keraterm facility and the transferring of persons from Keraterm facility to Omarska. It is of note that in this document, there is a slight change in wording. The Prijedor states Omarska was placed under the direct control of the police and the army. The Banja Luka CSB reports states, in the same decision, the Omarska facility was placed under the direct supervision of the police and army. I cannot account for that change in language. Again, it just continues by talking about the establishment of the centre and details, and in the centre and at the bottom of the report, it once again talks about numbers and the categorisation of prisoners. So this document, in essence, is a synthesis of the Prijedor report that was, I believe, sent up to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this, Your Honour, is an existing exhibit, S152.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could go back to the side, Mr. Brown, and if you could take us through that, I think it essentially shows similar matters referred to on the slide on Omarska.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again this just highlights some of the issues that I've just discussed in the report. It also highlights a couple of other references indicating that the military police were involved or engaged in the security of Keraterm camp, and there is documentary reference that the 1st Krajina Corps were aware of maltreatment of prisoners in Keraterm and that killings had occurred during a reported escape attempt in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move now to the next slide. I think most of the documentary references that support this slide have already been referred to, but if you can just take Their Honours through this slide. I know there's one document that we need to refer to at the end, but perhaps we can go through the slide first.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is simply a synthesis of some of the information which came from the police report. A figure of 5.000 was indicated in the 1st Krajina Corps report of the 1st of June. The police reports indicate the reception centre was established in late May. Again, security was provided by the military. I think I made reference to that yesterday. There's documentary evidence that joint military police convoys taking persons from Trnopolje to Central Bosnia occurred, and one of the references I think we're going to look at indicates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to that document, that is a document of the 18th of July of 1992 from Prijedor Public Security Station. And for the benefit of the interpreters, this is, in English, 00916561, and the Serbian version follows immediately thereafter. First of all, Mr. Brown, where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was seized by the OTP in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could highlight the relevant part of this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Prijedor Public Security Station document dated the 18th of July, to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre and the duty operations officer. And it states: "It has been arranged that a convoy of five (5) buses with women and children from the war-stricken area of Prijedor depart from the reception centre in Trnopolje (Prijedor Municipality) on the 18th of July, 1992, at 1000 hours. This has been arranged with Colonel Arsic of the Prijedor Garrison, and Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Peulic, commander of the 122nd Brigade. Since the destination of the convoy is Skender Vakuf, a police patrol from the Banja Luka Public Security Station will need to meet with the convoy at Tunjice and take it by safe road to the designated destination. A patrol car from the Prijedor SJB and policemen serving as escorts will be leading the way for the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And there's a Duty Officer signature block. Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Peulic, commander of the 122nd Brigade, why would he need to be involved in the arrangements for this convoy?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bosko Peulic was concurrently commander of operational group Vlasic. That was an operational group discussed yesterday, a number of groups below the corps. He commanded that 122 brigade, and was as well commander of operation group Vlasic in the Mount Vlasic feature in that area. I believe he was referenced in this document because the convoy was travelling through his zone. And Skender Vakuf was where Colonel Peulic's headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have to slow down a bit, Mr. Brown. It's probably my fault; I'm going too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. President, this document could be admitted into evidence, I believe it's 354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S354.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. Brown, we could now move to your next slide. Now here, I believe this slide is a sort of bullet point representation of events that took place in Prijedor after the end of May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, military activity did not stop with the events at Kozarac but continued after that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in terms of the first event, attack in Prijedor, by about 80 non-Serbs, if you could place on the ELMO the 1st Krajina Corps command report of the 30th of May of 1992. Again, this is a 1st Krajina Corps command regular combat report to the main staff. This is a seized document from the Bosnian Serb military authorities in Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you highlight the relevant portion of this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document makes reference to the attack on Prijedor by non-Serbs on the 30th of May. Section 1 states: "At 0400 hours on the 30th of May, paramilitaries of Muslim nationality attacked a position on the Sana River bridge, killing two sentries and then moving on to the hotel where they killed a member of the security and attempted to set the hotel on fire but were prevented from doing so. These events were followed by intensive actions in the town of Prijedor, and the Muslim extremists are attacking most fiercely from Donja and Gornja Puharska." The report makes additional references in paragraph 3. There's a small reference in paragraph 2 which I won't read out. Paragraph 3 states: "In the morning at about 0400 hours, a group of Muslim extremists neutralised a position at the Sana River bridge (killing two sentries), overpowered the Hotel Prijedor security guards and, using a molotov cocktail, set fire to the hotel where the military police was accommodated. After that, sniper fire was opened from several firing positions in the vicinity of the hotel until 0730 hours. At the same time, a group of eight extremists from the area of Donja Puharska opened fire on the targets in the barracks compound. Heavy fighting is taking place in the town of Prijedor itself. The assault was carried out by a group of about 18 Muslim extremists. In the wider area of Prijedor, mopping up and the process of disarming is continuing." The report also, in page 3, made reference that there had been some killed and several wounded, but because fighting had been -- was still in progress, they couldn't submit concrete data.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The report states that: "In the wider area of Prijedor, mopping up and the process of disarming is continuing." Do you have any idea what "mopping up" means? I mean, it's clear what the process of disarming is, but do you know what "mopping up" is?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents themselves don't give a definition of what "mopping up" is, but it's a phrase that is routinely used throughout the military reports. Mopping up, for example, is referenced in the latter stages of Kozarac. I believe it's also referenced when they discuss the attack on Hambarine. I imagine it's joint military and police operations in order -- directed against non-Serb areas, in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've already referred in the documents, as regards the camps, that large numbers of individuals of various categories ended up in those camps. Would they have ended up in those camps as a result of these mopping up operations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you want to make any further references in this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference in paragraph 12 of page 3 which is a recommendation and stating that: "...the disarming of paramilitary formations and in the area of Prijedor, the surrounding and destroying of the Green Beret forces should be continued." And I believe that is what happened in the days after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could apply for this document to be admitted into evidence. It's 355, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, S355.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we can go back to the slide. Now the next two entries we're not going to use those particular documents, but we'll see later documents which essentially reflect the same information. But if you could explain to the Judges what you believe was taking place, looking at the documents, from the end of May into the beginning of June of 1992 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the 31st of May, the 1st Krajina Corps was reporting that the area of Prijedor was under control of its forces, indicating that the attack on Prijedor was not a particularly successful one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And here you're talking of the attack by non-Serb forces on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There are a number of documents into June in many of the combat reports indicating that the police and the military were engaged in mopping up operations, operations to neutralise, smash, or eliminate individual groups in the wider Prijedor area and that there were continuing military operations in the municipality into July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could look at the next document, which is the document dated the 4th of June of 1992. For the interpreters, this document, in the B/C/S version, is 00861547. It's a regular combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the main staff of the Bosnian Serb army. Mr. Brown, this is another document seized by the Office of the Prosecutor from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could highlight the parts of this document, and I think it essentially reflects what you've already stated.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 2 states: "Mopping up and the disarming of paramilitary formations are underway in the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc." Paragraph 3 states: "Crisis areas: Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Donja Vakuf are under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps units. The population is fearful and apprehensive of the possible escalation of new conflicts, and the pressure to move out is increasing."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What do you believe that sentence means, that "The population is fearful and apprehensive for the possible escalation of new conflicts, and the pressure to move out is increasing"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sentence itself doesn't make it clear on its own which section of the population is fearful and apprehensive. However, in respect of Prijedor Municipality, taking into consideration the events of late May, the movement into camps in late May, and that this report was talking about three or four days after the 1st Krajina Corps had referenced that thousands of people were in camps, that I would assess that this is in relation to the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could apply for that document to be admitted into evidence, that's 356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections. Admitted, S356.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move back to your slide, you then highlight on the 23rd of July of 1992 combined operations by the 1st Krajina Corps forces from Prijedor and Sanski Most in Brisevo, Kurevo, Stara Rijeka, and Stara Majdan.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At this time period, there was a combined operation in those areas involving units from Prijedor and a brigade or elements of a brigade from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could place the document dated the 18th of June of 1992 onto the ELMO. Now, this is a document from the command of the 6th Partizan Brigade. Whereabouts did we get this document from?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was provided by AID Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The 6th Partizan Brigade, what unit was that subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 6th Partizan Brigade was subordinate to the 1st Krajina Corps, and it was based in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where was it -- you say it was based in the municipality of Sanski Most, that being directly south of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 6th Partizan Brigade in June and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Branko Basara was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you highlight for Their Honours the relevant portions of this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a combat order for the execution of combat activities. I draw your attention to the date that is annotated here as the 18th of June, and I'd like to come back to that in a minute. I'll read out the first paragraph or elements of it: "For the purposes of secrecy, groups of extremists are withdrawing from inhabited places to wooded areas where they are building dugouts using hunting lodges and carrying out training. At night, they go into inhabited places to pick up food and other materiel supplies. It is estimated that more numerous groups are located in - it's illegible but I believe it's Kurevo forest - around 100 Green Berets; Brisevo, up to 50; Carakovo, up to 30 extremists; and in the wider area of the Stara Rijeka opencast mine, about 50 extremists. For the purposes of coordinating with forces from Prijedor in combing the terrain in the area: Carakovo, Ostra Luka, Koprivna, Stari Majdan, Stara Rijeka, Ljubija, and Donja Ljubija, I hereby order..." And Colonel Basara orders elements of his brigade into combat operations in those areas. I draw your attention to paragraph 2, which states: "Destroy armed enemy groups with sudden fire, and take unarmed persons fit for combat to the Milim Birt area from where they will be transported onwards. Leave women and children and old men in their homes." He then outlines various tasks for his brigade, the military police, and the deployment locations for those units. I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 5: "All units must establish communications with Prijedor units before emerging in front of their positions and shall coordinate actions in the search, particularly in the settlement of Donja Ljubija, Ljubija, Stari Majdan, and others." Attached to this document, Your Honours, was a handwritten new order from Colonel Basara which I'd like to put up. This was handwritten the 22nd of July, 1999. I'd like to go back to the original order which is handwritten 18th of June. It is possible that the operation was scheduled for the 18th of June but was actually delayed until the 22nd of July. I believe Colonel Basara has got the date wrong or it's slightly illegible and it's 1992. It is possible that he got the handwritten date wrong and it wasn't, in fact, the 18th of June but the 18th of July. And I say this because the 1st Krajina Corps daily combat reports of the 23rd of July indicate that this operation was ongoing in this area. So although there are some difficulties in terms of date with this -- those two documents, I believe that the new order indicates that the operation was to take place on the 23rd of July. But the daily combat reports of the 1st Krajina Corps on that -- at that period indicate that an operation was taking place on the 23rd of July. The new order that Colonel Basara states includes establishing communications on the 23rd of July, that Prijedor troops will start the search at 0800, identification is to be facilitated with two red tapes on the shoulders of the troops. He does, in this instruction, state: "Don't fire unnecessarily. Do not set fire to houses. Looting is forbidden. Leave the population alone if they are peaceful. Lock up the extremists and liquidate armed groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I apply for that to be admitted into evidence. That's 357.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It goes -- we have some difficulties with these documents. First, may we hear, where and when did you find the documents? And what brings you to the conclusion that this handwritten was attached to the other document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm unclear of the date the document was received by the OTP. I believe it came from AID Bihac. And I believe that an investigator from the OTP copied the document. Further than, that I'm unable to give you an answer. It may well be the investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, this is not helpful at all. We need -- first, we have objections, standing objections by the Defence, all documents coming from this sort of AID. Second, there's evidently a discrepancy between the dates on the handwritten part and on the other part, therefore, it's doubtful whether or not these documents were ever together. And therefore, I regard it as necessary that the Prosecution finds out on the way of this FFI [sic] sourcing possibility you have to trace really where was this document found, was it really attached to this document, and so on. This is one obstacle. Second, document by document, and hearing just the comments of the witness on this document, this concrete document, we should be aware, and maybe this facilitates the work of the Defence as regards the cross-examination later, may I ask you, do you have any evidence or even hint that there was a link of influence by Dr. Stakic to the 1st Krajina Corps, to the 3rd Infantry Battalion, to Colonel Basara? Because we should never forget that we are discussing individual criminal responsibility; therefore, this question, do you have such a hint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any documentation that would indicate a link between Colonel Basara and Dr. Stakic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same is true for the 1st Krajina Corps and the 3rd infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen in the documents I've reviewed from the 1st Krajina Corps a reference to Dr. Stakic. There are the general references relating to civilian cooperation, and there is a reference, I believe, of a meeting that took place on the 7th of May, 1992, with municipal leaders. This is referenced in 1st Krajina Corps documentation, but does not indicate which municipal leaders or specify individuals. So I have not seen documentary reference from the military documents relating to Dr. Stakic outside the references, some of which were highlighted yesterday, relating to civil-military cooperation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind these reservations, the document as such is, as there are no objections, admitted into evidence as S357, and cautioned by the divergencies and the problems with content of especially the date of the handwritten document, the handwritten document has the exhibit number 357-1. It is now admitted into evidence, but as you know, it does not mean that we can decide the other way around. If not, we have, yes, the sourcing of this document and really know whether or not this was an attachment and where it was identified and found. Therefore, I expect an answer to these questions until the end of the week. Please proceed. Finally, the B/C/S version is in a relatively bad quality. Is it readable for you, Dr. Stakic, or do you need a better copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It seems to be adequate enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you would go to the third from last page and the very last page, you'll find that there is a certification from an individual called Jutta Paczulla who was an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor who states that she inspected this document on the 12th of April of 1996 in Bihac in the AID office. She returned the original to the AID for presentation. That certification is signed 5 November, 1996, by her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But nevertheless, we need, in this case, the best possible original to be presented in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that's going to be a photographic copy, Your Honour, but we'll get the best original that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may only add one point, Your Honour, since we are going through this process, and that is if we can get an explanation from the OTP or the individual who obtained those documents, why was there a lag time of actually reviewing the documents in April and then certifying those documents in November? If indeed it's accurate, although it's a preprinted form, that stamp that we've just referred to, the document should have been certified immediately upon the inspection, or I'd like to at least inquire how good is the memory of an individual of a handwritten document to make such a statement more than six to nine months after she has reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's discuss it when we have the best possible original at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, as far as this operation referred to and this document that's being questioned, have you seen any documents, for example, seized from the Banja Luka Corps, that would confirm that these operations took place? In other words, from a source which perhaps could be regarded as more reliable?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I stated, the daily combat report, this period, makes reference to operations in those areas. Those daily combat reports were seized by the OTP as part of the Krajina Corps archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So that would tend to make you question less the authenticity of S357, the order from the 6th Krajina Brigade because you viewed a document, as it were, from an original source or from a better source?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Although we're not actually referring to that document, I think, Mr. President, because of the matter you've raised, it may be one that's worthwhile putting into the package at the end because that will perhaps assist Your Honours' in determination of the authenticity of the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the final document on this, and if you could move your slide on. And I think that is the combat report that you referred to there, 24, 25 July, 1992, 1st Krajina Corps reports noting operations in Mount Majdan, Ljubija, Kozara, Kozarusa, Carakovo, Zecovi, and Kaljevo.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If you'd like me to find the footnote in my report, I can do. I can do that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll find that document. Now, in late August of 1992, you state the 1st Krajina Corps reports war crimes during mopping up operations in Carakovo and elsewhere. You've placed that document, I think, onto the ELMO. Now, first of all, where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps archive, seized in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an information report sent from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps forward command post to Prijedor operative group command, to the commander personally. And it forwards in entirety a report that the 1st Krajina Corps have clearly received. The document, in essence, states that the situation in Prijedor is particularly bad and notes specifically that there were divisions between the military police company and the command security platoon, and makes references to various military personnel in those units and the animosity between the two. It also makes reference to the Reconnaissance and Sabotage Company which had once been commanded by a Major Zoran Karlica. And I draw your attention to the last section and to page 2. It states: "The Reconnaissance and Sabotage Company, once commanded by Major Zoran Karlica, has an especially bad name in Prijedor. Since his death, the reputation of the company has constantly plummeted. Its members are nowadays best known for demolishing catering establishments in Prijedor, and in their last rampage they wrecked eight cafes owned by persons of Serbian nationality. On that occasion, the Military Police Intervention Platoon was disarmed by members of the Reconnaissance and Sabotage Company which has been joined since Karlica's death by dealers and war profiteers. This company with numerous murders of civilians, looting, private murders, et cetera. Its members also stood out in the mopping-up action in Carakovo by killing civilians, ripping earrings from women's ears, et cetera." Page 2 of the report continues: "Another interesting item - all are now washing their hands regarding camps and reception centres, attempting to pass responsibility for issuing orders for mass execution of civilians in the camps and centres onto someone else. This has become particularly noticeable since the visit of foreign reporters to Prijedor, more precisely to Omarska and Trnopolje. Forged (antedated) documents about all this are even appearing. However, the issue is sensitive and the sources are scarce, and more time will be required to complete this segment of the task. The impression is that the local Fatherland Front is involved in all this. "One thing is certain: We are already starting to feel the cost of the needless spilling Muslim blood. There is information that Muslims driven out of the municipality of Prijedor, and those who fled to the other side but who had done nothing against the Serbian Republic before, are now taking up arms in Croatia and joining the war against us. Several such persons were captured in Gradacac. In addition to this, Muslims who were either driven out of or fled from Prijedor to Croatia now attack everything that is Serbian, and the Serbs in Croatia have thus gained fanatical enemies, bequeathed to them by the civilian and military authorities of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So this was a document that you believe from its face was sent from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Prijedor operative group command in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And where, from this document, was the command of the 1st Krajina Corps based at that time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps was located in the Doboj area, hence the reason, I believe, the stamp says, "Command of the Doboj Operative Group 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that is up near the Croatian border. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's north of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's on towards the corridor area. The main command post of the corps had been collocated from Stara Gradiska to Manjaca camp in the summer of 1992. But a forward command post had been established in essence to deal with the combat operations in the corridor. The forward command post at times collocated with operations group Doboj which was another subordinate operations group which conducted operations in the corridor area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I apply for this to be admitted into evidence, please, Mr. President. I think it would be 358.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to ask why, but I have, following the questions to the last documents, two questions here. In the beginning, it reads: "To Prijedor Operative Group Command, (To the Commander, personally)." Do you know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at some stage Colonel Zeljaja took command of the 343rd Brigade. Colonel Arsic was moved elsewhere. And he also became concurrently commander of Prijedor Regional Command. That is, Colonel Zeljaja. I'm unclear when that transition occurred, but I believe by this period, the end of August, Colonel Zeljaja was in command of Prijedor region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. My second question is when you turn to the B/C/S version, you find a number of signatures or paraphs. Did you ever try in this case or in another case to identify these paraphs you can find there starting from 1945 until 2230? And is it possible that the four paraphs are all the same and would this be normal in the chain of command that one and the same paraphs appears four times on the same documents for the person receiving, evidently, the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the four signatures may well be those of the signaller that dispatched the document rather than the signatory of the document itself. The large box, stamp box, Received, Processed, Submitted, normally refers to the possibly a duty officer or an operator in the communications centre or possibly within the administrative section of the headquarters who actually disseminates and processes the document. At first glance -- I'm not a handwriting expert, but at first glance, the signature does look the same. And it is possible that these signatures relate to the communications technician or the duty officer who dispatched the document and archived it within the headquarters and may have logged it in a signal log book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So from your point of view, as a specialist, this would be nothing special and nothing that surprises you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, just for the record, because it might not be quite clear from the English translation, in the middle of the stamp, we find, once again, this four S. For the benefit of the transcript, once again, this stands for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I am unclear on the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the middle of the stamp, you can see four times an S in all the four directions. What does it mean? It's an abbreviation for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're referring to the Cs in the box and the cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would call it an S because it's Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I believe that is a symbol, a Serbian symbol, that is used. I am unclear on the actual translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then this document is ripe for admission as S358A. But the B version, once again we have a problem we had earlier. Here, we have indeed non-legible pages. Apparently, it seems to be the same problem, and if we can agree that somebody tried to copy both sides, and therefore, yes, we have to delete two illegible pages from the B/C/S version. Can the parties agree on this assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please delete these two pages, and the rest is admitted as S358B. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we could now move to your next slide. Before we actually look at, I think, two documents here, do you have any general comments to make about army and police cooperation in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the references we've already seen and the material that I have reviewed, I believe that army and police cooperation was very strong in Prijedor Municipality, including the use of police during combat operations. Some of that has been highlighted already. There was a requirement from the 1st Krajina Corps that there should be good cooperation with the police, and there were directives discussing the use of police in combat operations as well as references of joint operations involving police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we look at the document of the 29th of May of 1992. This is a 1st Krajina Corps document seized from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka by the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we look at paragraph 2 of that document. Could you read that sentence out that you've highlighted there.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Cooperation with the SR BH MUP, Ministry of the Interior, in mopping up the terrain and confiscating weapons from illegal formations in the area of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc continues."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could apply for admission of this document into evidence as 359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections. Admitted into evidence as S359.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now briefly look at the next document, which is a document of the 14th of June. Now, again, this is a regular combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the main staff of the 14th of June, 1992, seized by the Office of the Prosecutor from the archive of the Banja Luka Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. In this particular combat order, the Corps outline all he operative groups, and many of the units of the corps, and summarises what they are doing at the time. In relation to Prijedor, on page 2, it states: "The Prijedor operations and tactical group, including the 2nd Motorised Brigade, and the HAD of the 343rd Motorised Brigade --" the HAD was a subordinate artillery formation of the brigade -- "and the 6/10 PD --" the 6th being the 6th Brigade that we discussed earlier from Sanski Most, volunteers and the police secures the Bosanski Luka, Prijedor/Sanski Most/Sanica and Sanski Most/Bosanska Krupa routes, and deals with the remaining enemy troops in the areas of Kozarac village, Prijedor, and Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just go back to your slide briefly, I know you cite to other references in your report, but in essence, these two particular reports led you to the conclusion that there was army and police cooperation in Prijedor during the operations that are referred to in these documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, along with other police documentation which highlights a similar thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just go to the next part of your slide and whilst we won't pull these documents out, and if you could just briefly go through these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The last document was not tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S340. No objections. Admitted into evidence as S340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. 360.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could briefly go through these three bullet points.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, this just highlights another three examples of police cooperation. I believe they are referenced as footnotes in the report, CSB reports noting that Prijedor SJB directly took part in operations with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think we've seen that document, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have: There was a Prijedor SJB report summarising the activities of the Prijedor in late -- I think the last nine months of 1992. It's actually written in January 1993. Again, indicating the use of police in combat operations. And just a latter document in 1993 which was an open-source tribute to police officers who had died and it included references that there had been involvement with the military in combat operations in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Move to the final slide, Mr. Brown. Now, this one, in similar fashion to the last one, you've entitled "Army/Civilian Cooperation in Prijedor." Do you have any general comments before we look at some specific documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think much of this I covered yesterday in relation to cooperation with civilian authorities, army and civilian cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could just look at two, I think, existing exhibits in the case. First one being S59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which was read out already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Bearing in mind what the president has just stated, what does this document demonstrate to you for the purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a document by Branko Djeric, which was, in essence, instructions on the work of municipal Crisis Staffs. And what I wanted to do here was just highlight some of the issues relating to military issues from that instruction which I believe was implemented or broadly implemented in Prijedor Municipality. Paragraph 2 indicates that the president will consist of members, including the president, deputy president, and the commander of the Territorial Defence staff, and head of the MUP. Paragraph 3 states: "The Crisis Staff coordinates the functions of authorities in order to ensure the defence --"

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "... in order to ensure the defence of the territories, the safety of the population and property, the establishment of government, and the organisation of all other areas of life and work." Djeric's instruction stated that the command of the TO and the police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff, and therefore any interfering regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented. The instruction also states, in paragraph 11: "The Crisis Staff shall gather information concerning the field situation and inform and consult the competent bodies of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the government commissioners appointed for the areas especially threatened by war." I believe the Djeric instruction indicated that the Crisis Staff did have a general responsibility in the area of defence, that it certainly was a cooperative body in that respect, and that from this instruction, the Crisis Staff should have collected and gathered information regarding the situation on the ground. And it did have the requirement to have, certainly at this stage, a Territorial Defence presence. This instruction was written on the 26th of April at a time when the status of the JNA had yet to be resolved. I think that date is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Because at that time the JNA was still a federal body, not linked to any particular emerging republic within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the last document that we can refer to, which I think will bring us up to the break, and this document, for the purpose of the record, is S180.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again, Mr. President, I believe this has been read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have enough not to read out the entire Official Gazette, but in part. I don't know to which number you are referring here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's only, I think, four articles in this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is part of the Official Gazette of Prijedor and refers to a decision on the organisation and work of the Prijedor Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see the document as such. It is not from the Official Gazette, I think. It's issue number 2 -- okay, now I can see the top. Issue number 2, and indeed, yes. Please proceed because we are aware of this, and we read out this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How is this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How is this document relevant to your report, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I believe it shows that from the republic level down to the municipality level, these instructions were not simply just rarefied statements. Article 2 in the Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff instruction in essence was a direct lift from the Branko Djeric instruction in Djeric's paragraph 3 in that: "The Crisis Staff has been established in order to cooperate the functions of --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To coordinate.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, "to coordinate the functions of the authorities, the defence of the municipal territory, to protection of the safety of people and property." The Prijedor Gazette, in Articles 5 and 6, relate also to similar instructions from the Djeric document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I recall that this part was already admitted as Exhibit S111.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. So not S180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's both. We have the underlying document, and then the publication in the Official Gazette --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to be more specific. Thank you for the assistance, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Articles 5 and 6, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 5 states: "In accordance with the assessment of the political and security situation, and realistic requirements, the Crisis Staff shall adopt relevant decisions on the organisation and work of the Municipal Assembly, its organs, and other municipal organs and local communes." Article 6 states: "In discharging its functions in the area of defence, the Crisis Staff shall, in particular, coordinate the work and activities of all components of All People's Defence; consider issues of mobilisation, development, and reinforcement of the armed forces and other organisations and foster their cooperation with other responsible municipal organs; on special request of the commander of the municipal TO staff deal with issues of supply requirements and funding sources for the TO; keep abreast of all aspects of the situation in the municipality essential for the waging of armed combat and take appropriate measures; monitor the implementation of the recruitment plan and, where necessary, take measures for successful implementation thereof." Article 9 also relates to cooperation with the army. Article 9 reads: "The Crisis Staff shall at all times cooperate with the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, civil defence, and public security, through the senior officers or organs of these institutions." And Article 11 notes: "The provision of the constitution, the law and decisions adopted by the assembly, the presidency, and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the responsible organs of the Autonomous Region of the Banja Luka Krajina have been and shall remain the foundation for the work of the Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Going back to the slide, I think that is the last slide in the presentation, any final comments? I think the documents, the other documents referred to, certainly the 21 May, 1992 document is a document that we've already looked at which talks about closest possible cooperation between the people in legal authorities within their zone of responsibility and the corps, the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is correct. I believe the Djeric instruction and the Prijedor Gazette decision on the organisation and work of the Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff clearly indicate that coordination and cooperation was an important feature of the Crisis Staff, and that there was a clear relationship between the military in the municipality and the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've finished my examination-in-chief. But I would just like to mention one thing which you mentioned yesterday, because I don't have access to this document. You wanted a particular document that the witness had referred to in respect of the 8316 Prijedor Territorial Defence. And the witness, I think, indicated yesterday that that document is only in B/C/S. But I would ask him if he could make that document available to us so I could put that into the package at the end of his evidence for the additional documents that you've requested should be put in the file. I'll agree to that with Mr. Ostojic so he doesn't have any objections to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be excellent if only orally you could inform us on the content of this document, maybe before the cross-examination that it may form part of the cross-examination later on. If you could do it during the break, it would be excellent indeed. Thank you. It's 11.00 sharp. Just in time. Let's have a break now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I give the floor to the Defence, let me make one comment and at the same time one request. It would be helpful if the Prosecution could provide us with an analysis of the word that we can read in the English version as "mopping up." I tried to find the meaning of this word. Of course, you can't find it in Black's Law Dictionary. I found in Webster's New Word Encyclopedic Dictionary. "Mop up," the meaning: "Clearing out or rounding up of scattered remnants of beaten enemy forces in an area." So I think as we did it with the word and the translation of "cleansing," here it should be necessary to come back to the original B/C/S word and to find out the scope of application on the translation of this word. And then finally, in the direction of the Defence, we conferred during the break and we found it necessary, also in order to facilitate and abbreviate, maybe, the cross-examination, that we, the Judges, are fully aware that what we heard was more or less a description of, say, the environment, maybe elements of crimes, of a crime committed, in the area without reasonable doubt. But we are fully aware of the limited link until now established to a certain extent - I mention it on the basis of one document - as regards Dr. Stakic. Therefore, it's not necessary to emphasise during the cross-examination this special point. We are aware of this, and we regard this report as an important report but, to a certain extent, already, please, my apologies in your direction because you were asked to do so as a kind of closing arguments. So please, the floor is for the Defence. And may we have, for the transcript, that now we have, in addition, in the group of the Defence team the secretary of the Defence union, Mr. Lukic. Congratulations in person to this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My name is John Ostojic, as you know. I represent, along with Branko Lukic, the accused Dr. Milomir Stakic. It has been brought to my attention that on at least one occasion that I may have spoken a little too fast during some cross-examination of witnesses. So as to avoid that, since we both speak English, I would ask if you could kindly wait for the entirety of my question before you provide me with your thorough and complete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And to facilitate your work, let's, please, go in the beginning in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, within your CV, you state that as part of your duties and responsibilities is to review these combat regulations and doctrine, as well as to review witness statements. I think it's actually the very last two words of your curriculum vitae. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as part of other tasks in relation to my work in the team, I do at times review witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For purposes of completeness, it's one of the factors you would incorporate in preparing and analysing the outcome of your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this particular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I recognise that you didn't do it in this particular report. And my question is to you for purposes of completeness, why didn't you, sir, review the combat regulations, the military doctrines from both the SFRY, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, why you didn't review the Bosnian BH constitution, why you didn't review the military laws on defence, why didn't you review the witness statements that are in the possession of the OTP in connection with clarifying the issues of both the arming of the Muslims as well as how and when checkpoints were put into place in the area of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was an argument, not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can restate the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with me the reason why you didn't review witness statements with respect to the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the requirements placed on me during the initial brief, that it was to be a documentary-based report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you point in the military documents that you have where any of the correspondents -- just for purposes of clarity, before I move on to the next question, your answer says that this was one of the requirements. In fact, what you're saying, if I'm correct, sir, one of the requirements was for you not to look at the witness statements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was to be a documentary-based report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I understood. Thank you. As I was starting to ask, can you point to the number of military documents which either Dr. Stakic has been copied on or sent to a military battalion, platoon, squadron, or corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the documents relating to the meetings that occurred in Prijedor, National Defence Council meetings, Crisis Staff meetings, or other references that relate to those, I've not seen a document in the military collection that has Dr. Stakic on the distribution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that significant at all? In your opinion, as an objective military analyst?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not necessarily expect Dr. Stakic, as a municipal figure, to appear in documentation, especially corps-level documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you expect to see it in any level, not just the corps level, if there was any responsibility from a hierarchical command structure?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer whether I would expect it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, if I may, to page 32 of your report, I think, where you tell us again a limitation, although not necessarily covered earlier yesterday or today, and that is that you state: "It is not within my remit --" or "It is not within the remit of this report to analyse the detailed functioning of the Serb Crisis Staff, although some general comments should be noted." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that also a limitation of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's a limitation, and the documentation I used in relation to the Crisis Staffs, I concentrated on their issues or points that related to defence matters and not necessarily every aspect of Crisis Staffs; their function, their establishment, their history, their role, and where they fitted in throughout the whole of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time create a hierarchy of the MUP, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, or review documents in connection with establishing what that hierarchy is?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't establish a hierarchy of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In particular, the remits of the paper were about military activity. However, through looking at documentation, it is evident that there certainly was a chain that ran from Prijedor SJB to Banja Luka CSB, and the documents that we've reviewed over the last day would indicate that. But as to the detailed structure of the Bosnian Serb MUP, with all its facets, was not within the scope of this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're familiar, sir, are you not, in having reviewed other matters and materials, that Article 3 of the law of the military defence has a provision which suggests or clearly states that there's a principle of unity command between the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that unity of command was a principle of both the JNA and the VRS, and that unity of command was not limited exclusively to the army and the police. Unity of command referred to a unity of, as we have discussed earlier on, political direction. But I'm aware of unity of command within military doctrines of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that the unity command doctrines of the JNA that you reviewed do not include that a local politician from a municipality such as Prijedor would have any influence or control or direction involving either the military or the police which we've interchangeably, I think, called the MUP? M-U-P; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to review the doctrinal manuals again. I would argue in this particular case, in the period that we're discussing, that local political figures did have an influence on events, and not just local political figures, but those at a senior level. And to somehow argue that there was a ruthless separation between the military and the political figures and that they had no influence at all is not an assessment I would support from the documentation that I have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Since you're giving an objective report, and not knowing exactly what the Defence may be, are you being perhaps presumptuous that, in fact, the position as you state it would be the position of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not making any presumptions at all in that. But your questions, and not just the last one but other ones, you're discussing about political/military relationship. All I can say in that respect, from the documentation that I've seen, is that there clearly was a relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that relationship was, as you defined it, as being limited, is it not, limited to being just that of "influence of events." Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say it's more than simply influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are examples from the documentation that I've seen that show close coordination, close cooperation, a flow of events from republic through region through municipal level that ended up with action on the ground involving police and military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you see in the documents that you reviewed that Dr. Stakic ever gave an order to a military personnel or to a police officer to perpetrate or to commit any crimes whatsoever in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documentation I've seen, no, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You and I both know, sir, that, in fact, when you use words such as "cooperation" and "coordination" they indeed have military significance, do they not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in fact, when you use the word "cooperation" as you do within your report, it indicates what?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only a word that I use, but obviously the documentation reflects that as well. Cooperation involves a number of bodies working together, some kind of mutual support with a common aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And militarily speaking, "coordination" would mean what?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ensuring that military tasks are completed in a unified manner and receiving the support from bodies that can support that or support them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But is it true, sir, that in the military regulations and doctrines that you reviewed, there's a clear and distinct distinguishment between the words "coordination" and "cooperation"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are both used.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if they are used in the documents that you reviewed, sir. And regrettably, some of the translations you and I together may not agree upon. I'm asking you specifically within the combat regulations and the doctrines that you've reviewed and have apparently relied upon, do you know whether or not there is a clear distinction distinguishing the words "coordination" and "cooperation"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that in both military documents and in, for example, the Crisis Staff document the 20th of May, that "coordination" and "cooperation" are used. They are used as separate words in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: These nonmilitary people who may have used the word "coordination," do you know whether or not they knew what the significance that was as it may relate to the military doctrines and regulations that you rely upon and that existed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the witness can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, do you agree with Philip Coo, who says that on page 10.079 of his testimony recently, that in fact the word "coordination" has command implications but the word "cooperation" does not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I probably would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in your Power Point presentation, when you talk about the cooperation of the military and the civilians, can I -- sorry. If you can just put it on your laptop, and then we can see it. It says "Army/civilian cooperation Prijedor." May I be presumptuous and infer that in fact, based upon your definition, based upon what the law was at that time, based upon your experience, that in fact the cooperation that you cite for us under that caption, which was the last, I think, slide that you presented, in fact, has no command implications?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, if it facilitates, I was told the ELMO works now. So if you have a hard copy, maybe you can...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have one as well. Do we need to put it on?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps for those who may not have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps for those who do not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This slide here? It does say "cooperation" in the slide. However, some of the references that I've highlighted, in particular, the 20th of May, 1992, instruction makes reference to coordination as well as cooperation. Possibly the slide should read "coordination" and "cooperation."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you for that. But I think in your objective analysis, you didn't include it. And I think if you look at the objectiveness of the fact that there's a distinguishment between those two words, that in fact when you use the word "cooperation" here, it has, as I've stated earlier without getting an answer, it has no command implications. Correct? We'll break it down one by one in a second, but if I can get the answer to that question, I'd be happy to move along.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that other documentation indicates coordination as well as cooperation. I would accept that cooperation may not on its own indicate a command relationship, and that coordination is certainly a stronger word and may well indicate command relationship, or potential command relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: Do you know if there's a difference between what's known as a staff organ and an organ that is engaged in commanding?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, there is a commander, and a commander will have a staff. Staff are there to, in essence, facilitate a command function of that commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, sir, does the staff organ and the people within that, the staff of officers supporting the commander in exercising of his command responsibilities themselves, do they have command responsibility or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would argue that in some cases they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if I share with you that on page 10.119 of Mr. Philip Coo's testimony recently he argues quite the opposite, you would disagree with him. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read what he said, if you can put that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. "The commander is the individual with command responsibility; the staff organ is the staff of officers supporting the commander in the exercise of his command responsibilities but they themselves do not have command responsibility." Again, I think it's 10.119 is the page number of the transcript in the case of, for the Court, the OTP versus Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would argue that, under most circumstances, that was the case. There may potentially be times when a commander would issue instructions to subordinate staff officers for certain issues. As a general principle, I would probably argue - I'm not quite sure if I would be so emphatic - that in all circumstances, at all times, the staff would not be exercising some kind of command responsibility. However, it is the responsibility of the commander to command, and it is the responsibility of the staff to facilitate his orders and instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to stay with the ELMO and the Power Point presentation involving army and civilian cooperation in Prijedor to your right, you reference one particular document dated the 26th of April, 1992. Can you share with me, sir, with respect to this document by Mr. Branko Djeric whether or not paragraph number 4 of that document wherein it clearly states that there should -- let me read it to you just to make sure I have the quote. "The command of the TO and the police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff." Just for completeness, I'm going to read the whole thing. I have several questions on that point. And it proceeds to say: "And therefore, any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or the use of the police forces must be prevented" of paragraph 4. Are you familiar with that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
