utterances.text: Within this, when Mr. Djeric identifies -- just tell us again who he is so I have a complete appreciation for his position within the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you get that from the signature block. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He directed this Exhibit S59 -- I apologise, Your Honour, for not identifying it -- S59, he directed this to whom?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He directs the instruction to the Municipal Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir -- well, strike that. Let me ask this question first to get a better understanding of this paragraph. When Mr. Branko Djeric identifies that the TO and police forces and its command structure is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff, in your opinion as a military analyst having reviewed these documents and based upon your experience, who do you think he is identifying as a professional staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commanders of those particular units, the commander of the TO and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He's not referring to a local politician; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm assuming he's referring to the professional TO commander and the MUP commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Staff organs that we talked about earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the commanders within those organs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then when he proceeds to say: "And therefore any interference regarding the command of the TO and/or use of the police forces must be prevented," is it clear, sir, that he is giving an indication that there cannot be and must not be any interference with respect to command involved by those other than the professional staff vis-a-vis the TO and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does. However, I'd like to add that I don't believe in the Prijedor Crisis Staff document of the 20th of May that that particular section is replicated. And in relation to defence issues, on the 20th of May document, it states that in discharging its functions in the area of defence, the Crisis Staff, relating to Prijedor, shall coordinate the works and activities of all components of All People's Defence. And I believe that Branko Djeric's section is not contained within the Prijedor Crisis Staff decision of some one month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And had it been included within the Prijedor Crisis Staff May 20th, 1992, decision, being an objective military analyst, you would have simply come in here and told us under oath that, in fact, because this provision is included, that there was absolutely no command responsibility as it relates to Dr. Stakic and either the military and/or the police. Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't relate to the military in entirety; it relates to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll be glad to modify my question to the TO and to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it had been present, I would have had to take that into consideration. I don't think it's an unusual request, however. Djeric may well have been stating that, in essence, the military or TO, actually, and police had their roles to do, and that was their function. But I do find it somewhat interesting that it isn't in the Prijedor Crisis Staff and that Article 6 of the Prijedor Crisis Staff document does indicate issues of Defence and coordination with components of All People's Defence as well as other issues relating to military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar that in fact Mr. Branko Djeric is merely reciting the law as it existed at that time relating to the command responsibility and whose control and authority the MUP or the TO would have been in, having reviewed those VJ doctrines, the constitution, and other military defence materials of Prijedor and Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unsure if that's an exact replica of those regulations, and I would have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, do you have any inclination one way or the other whether that is the law as it existed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In where? Which law; RS or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina, which obviously related to the Prijedor Municipality, that in fact the exclusive authority of the TO and the police forces belongs to the professional staff and that no one must interfere and any interference must be prevented?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not quote specifically which part of Republika Srpska law that that might have come from, or is replicated in RS law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't find it an unusual issue in a way. The MUP are a profession. The military are a profession. And of course, there is one thing in relation to the law, there is another in relation to the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree. And when we discuss the law or the de jure responsibility of a local politician, would you agree with me that the law, as it existed at that time, in fact, clearly and unequivocally recited the fact that at the very least the TO and the police were under the exclusive authority of the professional staff as you've identified previously here today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness has already several times stated that he is not aware of this text, and it would not be responsible for the witness to answer on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, if I may, again, to your slide, your Power Point presentation. Under May 20, 1992, there, you in fact use the words, sir, that the Prijedor Municipal Assembly decision broadly implements Djeric's instructions, as opposed to, let's say, narrowly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prijedor decision on the 20th of May is significantly more detailed than the Djeric instruction. It adds in other articles that aren't contained within the Djeric instruction. But there's a broad similarity in the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that what you're trying to say with respect to that section, 20th of May, 1992, within this Power Point presentation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me here, sir, what the structure, since you indicate that there were some links, and what the hierarchal structure was of the MUP, starting with the chief of police within the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. President. He has already asked him this question. The witness explained what the hierarchy was in the MUP, so now he's repeating his questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I totally disagree that we were given a hierarchy of the MUP leading up from the Prijedor Municipality all the way through to the federal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness was asked, Mr. President, what the hierarchical structure was of the police. And the witness responded - I remember it very clearly - he stated, "I haven't done an exact study of that but I looked at the documents and I can tell you it went from Prijedor to Banja Luka Regional CSB headquarters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have the impression the former question was related to the MUP in general and now the question is on the hierarchy of the MUP only in Prijedor Municipality. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic has just mentioned the federal police. Now he's moving us towards Yugoslavia because that's where the headquarters of the federal police are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know, I know. Yes, let's try to understand this question, or Mr. Ostojic may rephrase the question. When indeed its limited to the Prijedor Municipality, it is admissible. When it's on the MUP in general, indeed, the question has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this, Mr. Brown, if you may: With respect to the Prijedor Municipality, do you know what the hierarchy was of the police?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within Prijedor police, I am unaware of the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if -- well, it's a difficult question but I'm going to ask you it anyway: You did mention that the Prijedor police reported to the CSB in Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you point in one document that you have from which you rely upon that the Prijedor MUP reported to the Municipal Assembly or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Point it out.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the -- not the Municipal Assembly as such, but the municipal SDS board meeting held on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just for a minute. We'll get to those documents in a second. If you could find a document specifically referencing that the police, the MUP in Prijedor, reported to the Crisis Staff during the time period that we're discussing and/or the Municipal Assembly from April 1992 through September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel that he gives the witness the opportunity to make reference to that document he wants to make reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, proceed as you wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document dated the 9th of May of the SDS municipal board meeting at which 32 members of the Prijedor municipal board attended was also attended by Simo Drljaca, the police chief. And he clearly is briefing those present on a number of issues and some concerns, one being that the TO should take over some responsibilities of guarding or protecting facilities. He briefs the municipal board meeting on negotiations that are ongoing in Ljubija and Kozarac and the extension of deadlines. He makes reference that the police are working on the prevention of smuggling and crime and makes note of the issues of salary payments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, if I may - I don't know if you're complete or not - that's SK46. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is. There are the other minutes which we have discussed in relation to the National Defence Council in Prijedor, which the police chief clearly is briefing those present on the situation in the municipality. And I believe we have gone over two of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are also the references in the establishment instruction of Omarska camp which discuss, as a result of Crisis Staff decisions, that an establishment instruction is sent to the Crisis Staff, or at least the Crisis Staff is on the distribution list. Those are a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to list all of them, but if you could confine it, if I may - and I thought my question was precise, I apologise if it was inarticulate - I'd like to see, and I couldn't -- I'd like to see which documents that you have that you're supporting to show that there's a link of some responsibility between the police, military, and the local politicians, the document from either the MUP or the military to the local politician or that organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm objecting because Mr. Ostojic characterises the question in such a way as if the witness hasn't actually answered the previous question, and the previous question was, "Are there any documents which indicate that the police were reporting to the Crisis Staff?" And the witness has very clearly demonstrated exactly that with this document, with this document of the SDS board meeting together with the Omarska establishment document in which Drljaca signs it, stating, "I'm setting up Omarska camp in accordance with the instruction of Crisis Staff." So he has answered these questions and I think we should move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After having conferred with my colleagues, sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed with the line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Within SK46, sir, do you not note that the intent at all times of Dr. Stakic within the specific time period in question clearly states what when he is referenced in quoting, that there should be war or that peace must be maintained at all costs? SK46, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this famous sentence is now in all our heads. It must not be restated and we have to discuss the importance of this sentence later, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Should I move on, Your Honour? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Should I move on, Your Honour? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, it doesn't make much sense. We have read these documents and the final evaluation is for us. And I think the witness gave a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the term "SUP" means, S-U-P versus M-U-P, or the acronym for that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: MUP is the Ministry of the Interior. The SUP, I believe, is the national security service. I may be wrong, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is what you think it means. From some of the documents we saw that there was an entity called a Secretariat of Internal Affairs, the documents that you relied upon. Do you, sir, know whether or not SUP in any way was the hierarchical link to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unclear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you also, sir, agree with me that because you're unclear of that you would also be respectfully unclear of what, if any, relationship local politicians may have within the SUP vis-a-vis the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was not part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn to another topic if I may, with the Court's permission. Militarily speaking, you are familiar with the term "rules of engagement," are you not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And militarily speaking, those rules of engagement constitute specific and precise manner in which military personnel would act under both noncombat and combat activities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, generally they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or, if I may be somewhat presumptuous, do the rules of engagement specifically are put in place during only combat activities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only in a position to give experience from my own military service where there are rules of engagement during peacetime as well as combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. With respect to some of the language that you've used in your report, and I note the deliberate manner in which you've done so, there are words such as "request" and "order." Those two words separate and apart have significant meanings within the purview of yourself such as a military analyst, do they not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with me, sir, what the difference is between a request and an order.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order is a direct command for action and, in military contexts, has something that normally is obeyed by subordinate units. A request is generally something less than that; a request for information. Having said that, requests do have a -- there is clearly a relationship that the request should be satisfied by a subordinate, but clearly an order I think is more emphatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, does not an order establish some sort of link whereas a request clearly does not? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, once again, these are two extremely judicial and also military judicial terms. And to define these terms both in the judicial context and in the military context, it's for the Judges to find the definition and not for the witness. I apologise, Mr. Brown, but this is an area we should have for ourselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, if I just may be heard on this point, briefly, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before you start, I thought we did overcome this period that we had in the beginning that we discuss strictly legal issues, yes, echoed by a witness. I think it's for the argument and for closing arguments maybe, or deliberations, to discuss these issues. But what there is an order, what there is a request, this is public domain. It's highly disputed in both areas, and therefore, it should be indeed for the Judges to find these terms. And one shouldn't make the attempt, it would be misleading, to discuss, for example, the distinction between "cooperation" and "coordination." This would be two sophisticated. And of course, the witness being not the author of the documents including these words cannot comment on this. And I can cast with a deluge of explanation on "request" and "order" and "cooperation" and "coordination"; it doesn't help much. The witness is not the author of these documents, and therefore we should refrain from these sophisticated distinctions helping us not one step further. But please, if you want to comment and to give an argument to the record, it's your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to make an argument. Actually, I am seeking some direction on that. The documents specifically offered and relied upon by Mr. Brown clearly have the language of request in the documents that he relates to the political establishment in Prijedor in 1992. Having been presented as a military analyst and knowing personally the significance of both the words "request" and "order," I think it's within the purview to establish whether or not that from a military standpoint may have significance. We're not asking at this time for the Court to decide on any threshold issues involving either "cooperation," "coordination," or "orders." However, once this witness, in my opinion, talks about it, I'm simply laying the foundation so that I wouldn't be accused later of being presumptuous as to what the words mean. I'm willing to go with his definition; I'd like to make a specific relationship with the documents wherein those words are specifically used. But nevertheless, I'm willing to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to this issue of rules of engagement, sir, are you familiar with what the rules of engagement are during combat activities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very general question, I think. I wonder if it could be pared down. I don't think there are general rules of engagement that, say, are all encompassing for all situations, for all military organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, it would depend on whether the military personnel were either provoked or attacked themselves, correct, as opposed to a military who's passing through, let's say a convoy on the Banja Luka/Prijedor main road on or about April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think rules of engagement are dependent on that type of scenario. Rules of engagement give guidelines to militaries where they are allowed to -- from my perspective where they are allowed -- the level of force that they are allowed to utilise in particular circumstances. Potentially in peace, potentially in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just clarify for the purposes of the record, what rules of engagement are we talking about? Are we talking about JNA rules of engagement? Or Are we talking about British army rules of engagement? Are we talking about the French army's rules of engagement? Because I think we need to be specific here if we're talking about what was happening in Prijedor, then there must have been rules of engagement that were issued by the JNA which Mr. Lukic and Mr. Ostojic presumably have and can be shown to the witness and then we can discuss it in detail, but to talk in generic fashion like this is, in my view, extremely misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I disagree. And I will tell the Court why, respectfully, to Mr. Cayley. This witness answered the foundational question. If Mr. Cayley would like to testify, let him so state. The witness recognises what is a well-known international terminology called rules of engagement which deals specifically with his area of expertise, having a background that he does. Specifically, it is that request that we hope to analyse the three or four instances of what has been identified in Mr. Brown's report as provocation as opposed to instigation, by others. But we'll get to that in due time. Mr. Brown didn't object or didn't hesitate to say that he is familiar with rules of engagement. Not only was he familiar with them, he knew what they were in peacetime and, as he says, wartime. And all we want to do is have an honest and objective discussion about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He's talking about his own experiences, Mr. President, [redacted], and I think it is misleading for Mr. Ostojic to transpose the rules of engagement with which this witness, [redacted], was familiar and to suddenly thrust those into the middle of Prijedor in 1992. If Mr. Ostojic has the rules of engagement of the JNA, of the VRS from that period of time, then let him put them to the witness, because rules of engagement, by and large, are written down. They are written, as are military regulations. So that is all I'm asking, because otherwise the record is extremely misleading and unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Indeed, once again, it doesn't help to go in sophisticated details of the definition of the one or other term indeed used here, used there, with another meaning. Therefore, indeed, it's the right of the Defence to discuss this issue, but related to the area in question and, indeed, to be objective, whether or not there are indicia that people followed these rules or not. This would be the question, and I anticipate already now some questions by the Judges. But indeed, it's not relevant what this notion means in general but are there any such rules to be found and how are they refined especially in the area in question? This is only the admissible question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then we will formally adopt that question, and if the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my analysis, Your Honour, I have seen no documentary evidence indicating what the rules of engagement were, either from the JNA during this period or after transition to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You discussed, sir, briefly in one of the documents and in your direct testimony yesterday and today briefly items concerning discipline and punishment of individuals. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which part you're referring to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just generally, sir, do you remember discussing that in any of the documents? Here's my question to you, and you tell me if you didn't discuss it, be very candid and tell me you didn't. What was the link, if any, of responsibility of a local politician to discipline a military personnel who may have acted outside his scope of duties and obligations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not address that in the report. I did not address that in my direct testimony yesterday or this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is the obligation, sir, of a local politician to punish a military personnel who may have acted outside of his scope of duties and obligations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness has answered this question and said that he didn't address this question. And it did not form a part of the testimony of yesterday or this morning. So I can't identify any foundation. And, yes, leave it with this. It's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The question was slightly different, Your Honour. And I'm not just not sure if the witness will give the same answer, and I was seeking to get three specific areas; punish -- or discipline first, punish, and then prevent. And I broke it down -- I thought I did it that way. If I misspoke, it's really I should include it as a compound question, which may raise the OTP to object that it's compound. But nevertheless...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Subject matter is no doubt the fourth amended indictment, and the question whether or not there was a kind of influence, possible influence, then, of course, you're right. Please proceed in this way, but the word "punish" never appeared until now, as far as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to this concept of influence, would you agree with me, Mr. Brown, that before any individual, including a local politician, would be able to influence a military person relating to military personnel that may have acted outside the scope and obligations of their duty, they would need to be informed clearly and precisely of what it is or what action it is that needs to be either disciplined, punished, or prevented. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. President, I don't know about the witness, but I don't understand that question at all, so can we break it down? It really doesn't make any sense whatsoever. It's compound, as Mr. Ostojic said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it facilitates also the answer of the witness if you can have certain portions, and then step by step approach. But in the meantime, may I ask, any objections to delete from the transcript you mentioned a certain country, and the profession?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm sorry, I apologise. And in fact the registrar kindly brought it to my attention and it should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please proceed step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, trying to proceed step by step, when you use the word "influence," can you tell me what influence a local politician would have to punish a military personnel who have acted outside the scope and obligations of their duties, such as committing a crime?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a general question, I'm assuming, rather than a specific one in relation, say, to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the Court was clear; we were going to confine it to that Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what influence a local politician would have to punish military personnel who acted outside the scope and obligation of their duties. Clearly, the military had prosecutorial process, but I'm unaware of what the legal responsibilities of a local politician would be in terms of influence. I would, again, add that in Prijedor, from the analysis of the material I have seen, there was close linkage between the military command, the police command, and the civilian authorities. And I believe that documentation shows that. There are references that in Prijedor, going on the 20th of May instruction, Crisis Staff instruction, that it was an obligation for the Crisis Staff to be kept informed of events on the ground in relation to defence matters. And other documents in relation to, say, the National Defence Council indicate, again, that linkage between the military, police and civilian authorities. And the discussions at those meetings clearly indicate that events in the area are being discussed. But as to your question on the legal responsibilities of a local politician, it is not addressed in my report and I have not analysed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Leaving for a moment aside the question of the responsibility and who is a politician in this sense, would you regard it as an influence to dismiss, for example, chief of police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe if the chief of police was dismissed on the instructions of a local politician, that clearly would be influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to add one other thing; that in relation to the Territorial Defence especially, that local politicians in former Yugoslavia municipal level did have significant influence on the issue of the Territorial Defence, both in the nomination of Territorial Defence commanders and in their general administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And under which law, statute, doctrine do you base this opinion on, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to check, and I cannot give you a law or statute at the moment. But in Prijedor, for example, Slobodan Kuruzovic was dismissed as Territorial Defence commander and placed under the command of Prijedor regional command by a Crisis Staff decision of the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, if I may, sir: With respect to document - and you can have it in front of you - S21 that we've previously identified and a document that was, I believe, admitted today, S359, do you have those two documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little unclear, the S numbers, what they would refer to because I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll identify it. S21 is a document that I think you identified as being from the Ministry of National Defence, dated the 16th of April, 1992. And I think Mr. Cayley asked you the source or reliability and integrity of the document, where you received it. And then comparing that with S359, which is a document dated -- I'm sorry. Actually, it's S358 that I'd like you to reference, which is a document dated August 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May it assist if I give you the footnote numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S21 refers to footnote number 15, and S358, footnote number 145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it assists the witness, please, the usher may present Document S358 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have both documents here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S21 and 358, you know what we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one is the 16th of April decision, and the other one is the 1st Krajina Corps forward command post report to Prijedor garrison command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Personally, it says, I think. Correct? Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "personally."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to identify it. Then that's correct. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in discussing S21, I know you identify the source as being AID in Bihac. If you look on the B/C/S, as we've identified it, document, it's added there in the Cyrillic script of a Latin-script text: "To all Serbian municipalities," is it not? I'll direct...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You as a military analyst being familiar with reviewing documents from the military police and political institutions, did that strike you, sir, as being something highly unusual, that here is a document in its formal manner, bearing a stamp, written in Latin script, that the words, "To all Serbian municipalities" is apparently typed in but yet in Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unusual. I would accept that. However, for me, the important document is the 4th of May document, or as important is the 4th of May document which refers to the 16th of April decision. And when that document is placed, as I did yesterday, with all the other ones, it would indicate that there was a passage of that instruction down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, examining Document S358 in the couple minutes that we have left, which was the document "To the Prijedor Operative Group Command (To the Commander Personally)" --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- that document certainly is significant, sir, is it not because it identifies that there are "forged (antedated) documents" that are circulating and that in fact individuals are trying to wash their hands regarding the camps? Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In connection with your analysis, your military analysis, did that, sir, play any part in determining whether or not any of the documents that you relied upon are indeed forged?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't in particular because the reference in that document states that it was "forged (antedated) documents" about the issue of camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's exactly my point, Mr. Brown. And in fact the documents that you rely upon on the establishment of both Omarska and Keraterm are the documents from the police and/or military that are otherwise - at least according to S358, people are trying to wash their hands - documents that the OTP seized five years after the events in question are surfacing, and those documents are purportedly suggesting to you that certain groups but not others established those detention centres and camps, namely, Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little unclear on the question. I wonder if you could rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. You, sir, rely on documentation that obviously is in existence that the OTP under a, in my opinion, in December of 1997 lawful search and seizure confiscated or took documents from various institutions in Prijedor five years after the period in question. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My point namely is that they did not, meaning the OTP or any entity, perform a search and seizure and confiscation of those documents at or around the time of their creation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Understanding as a military analyst that there is a five-year gap from the time of the events in question and the documents that were seized, in light of Exhibit S358, did that play a role, sir, in your analysis in determining who may have established the detention centres or camps, namely Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I believe that there are a number of documents from more than one source relating to detention centres and their existence from various dates. This document saying, "forged (antedated) documents" are even appearing gives no indication of how many, who is writing them, although it does make a reference to the Fatherland Front, and its sources are scarce and the issue is sensitive. I would find it difficult to believe that all the documents that have any reference to Omarska were somehow all forged.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that all of them do, sir. But did you during your analysis as a military analyst, did you take into account S358 while evaluating the report by the MUP which states that the Crisis Staff established the Omarska Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't believe that that was one of those documents being referred to in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, based upon your answer there, what documents do you believe do fall or are referenced by this report S358 that constitute a forgery?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It makes no reference to the documents. It just throws up that maybe appear or are appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can turn briefly to one other issue in the limited time that we have today, and that is the May 30th, 1992, attack on Prijedor by the Muslim Bosniaks, if you will. You might need S358 still. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, sir, and are you familiar with who actually on May 30th are the people who perished in the attack by the Bosniak Muslims on the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the Bosniaks or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Either one.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a list of some of the soldiers in one of the documents who were killed during that attack. There's also a list of, I believe, five police officers who were killed on that period, and I'm assuming that they were killed as a result of that combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact, sir, that Major Zoran Karlica was also killed during the attack of the town of Prijedor on May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, in light of Exhibit S358 that, in fact, that as Mr. Zoran Karlica's unit, that because of the fact that he was killed on May 30th, decided, as it says here, to commit numerous murders of civilians, looting, private murders, et cetera; its members also stood out in the mopping up action. And it continues to describe that since his death, since the death of Major Zoran Karlica, the unit had a reputation which has constantly plummeted?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the document says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Keeping that in perspective, if you will, and in the proper context, what link does the MUP or what authority would the MUP have with respect to this unit that has apparently gone off on its own and has, for one reason or another, decided to commit these tragic crimes?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that if the MUP were aware that those crimes had been committed, that they would have had some responsibility in investigating those crimes and informing the military authorities of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if they were not aware, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly, if they were completely unaware of the crimes, they are unaware of the crimes. And they would presumably not be in a position to initiate an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They would have no responsibility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say if they would have no responsibility. There may -- I would assume -- maybe I'm straying out here of my report. But it is the function of the police to detect and report crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just, in the minute or two that I have left, if I may, with the Court's permission, same question with respect to the political establishment in Prijedor in 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can only go back on what I've said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, it would be the same answer that you previously gave in connection with the MUP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In relation to the question you asked some time ago on the responsibilities of civilian authorities to punish, I'm unaware of the responsibilities of civilian authorities. And all I can say is that from the documentation that I've seen, civilian authorities had a responsibility, according to the 20th of May instruction certainly, to keep abreast of situations on the ground and that there was cooperation between military police and civilian authorities in the documentation I've reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, are you saying that the political establishment had more responsibility than the MUP did in investigating?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say I don't know the responsibilities that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, it might be a convenient time now in light of the Defence's scheduled meeting with Dr. Stakic at 6.00. But I'm not sure -- again, we'll proceed in the manner the Court wishes obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think no doubt this was the reason we scheduled the possibility for having other visiting time for 6.00. Dr. Stakic has to be brought to the Detention Unit first. And let's stop immediately now. One last-minute information I just got: Tomorrow, we will sit in Courtroom II from 9.30 to 1.00 and from 2.30 to 4.00. And once again, this allows you to contact Dr. Stakic immediately after this. But in addition, to prepare a decision, may I have the submissions by the parties. It's the intention of the Tribunal to proceed Friday morning under Rule 15 bis due to the fact that Judge Fassi Fihri will not be available on Friday morning. It's just a question of a right to be heard before we prepare our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection on the side of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance. May I also hear...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, we agree, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes today's hearing. Thank you, Mr. Brown. You see it's necessary to continue tomorrow morning. And the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.30.
